compressed_text: Volkswagen announced on September 26, 2025, that it will suspend production for one week in early October at its Zwickau and Dresden EV plants in Germany, citing market conditions. Bloomberg also reported a brief shutdown at its Emden plant, which VW did not confirm. The move reflects weak European EV demand due to high upfront costs and sparse charging infrastructure. Bosch recently announced German workforce cuts partly due to weak EV demand, while Ford plans up to 1,000 job cuts at its Cologne EV plant. Volkswagen's Zwickau and Dresden sites produce the ID. family and Audi Q4 e-tron. The automaker previously struck a union deal to cut 35,000 jobs by 2030, facing fierce competition in China and weak European demand.

In August 2025, Honda's global auto production fell to 267,005 units (87% YoY), continuing a 13-month decline. Japan production dropped to 44,586 units (88.4% YoY), the first YoY fall in three months; January–August Japan output was 438,531 units (98.5% of 2024). Production outside Japan decreased to 222,419 units (86.7% YoY), marking the 13th consecutive monthly decline; year-to-date outside Japan was 1.84 million units (90.2% of 2024). North America produced 136,559 units (94.9% YoY), and Asia 76,887 (74.3% YoY). In contrast, exports from Japan surged to 7,307 units (up 126.9% YoY), the fifth consecutive monthly increase. North America received 2,037 units (up 270.2% YoY). Japan’s domestic new vehicle sales dropped to 301,221 units (8% YoY decline).

On October 16, 2025, BMW reported that parts of its supplier network are affected by a trade and intellectual property dispute over chipmaker Nexperia, which faces export restrictions in both the U.S. and China. BMW stressed that production continues as planned and it is assessing supply risks. Mercedes-Benz is monitoring the situation; Volkswagen said its production is unaffected. Nexperia, a major supplier of basic automotive chips, is seeking talks over the restrictions. The Dutch government took control of Nexperia, citing technology transfer concerns with its Chinese parent Wingtech. Most Nexperia chips are assembled in China.

On October 17, 2025, the European auto association ACEA warned that a dispute between China and the Dutch government over chipmaker Nexperia could severely disrupt European vehicle manufacturing. On October 4, China’s commerce ministry prohibited Nexperia China from exporting specific components; the Dutch government had taken control of Nexperia on September 30, citing technology transfer risks. Nexperia, fully owned by China’s Wingtech (on the U.S. entity list since December), notified carmakers it could no longer guarantee chip deliveries. Without these high-volume chips, European suppliers cannot produce parts, risking production stoppages.

Ford slashed its F-150 Lightning workforce in Dearborn to one-third of 2,100 employees, with the rest transferred or offered early retirement, due to a dual crisis: plummeting EV demand and the Sept. 16 fire at Novelis' Oswego mill—supplying 40% of U.S. automotive aluminum—halting operations until early 2026. Ford prioritized gasoline F-series trucks, idling EV production. The aluminum disruption could cost $500M–$1B in lost earnings and threaten Super Duty output. Ford's stock dropped 10% since the fire. Analysts warn of extended wait times and broader economic risks as the EV revolution falters and subprime auto loans show strain.

On October 21, 2025, General Motors Canada announced it is ending production of the BrightDrop electric delivery van at the Cami plant in Ingersoll, Ontario, which has operated for over 30 years. The decision, driven by poor sales (about 2,000 units in 2024), leaves approximately 600 workers’ future uncertain after layoffs and a semiconductor shortage. Union representatives were blindsided, calling it devastating. GM is not moving production elsewhere but assessing future opportunities for the plant. Industry experts warn the plant’s fate may be sealed unless a new model arrives, complicated by U.S.-Canada trade war tariffs and the upcoming CUSMA renewal. Federal and provincial officials formed a response group to push for new production.

On October 14, 2025, the Netherlands invoked its Goods Availability Act to intervene in Chinese-owned Nexperia, citing economic security. In retaliation, China barred Nexperia’s China arm from exporting certain chips. GM CEO Mary Barra warned on October 21 of potential production disruptions. Volkswagen flagged possible temporary outages due to the restrictions. The European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association cautioned that Nexperia chip stocks may last only weeks, with alternative sourcing taking months. Honda is assessing impacts. A Japanese distributor reported a fivefold surge in orders for chips from other manufacturers like Texas Instruments amid supply fears.

King will attend the dedication ceremony for the United Kingdom's first memorial honoring LGBT armed forces personnel, as reported on 2025-10-27. Global automakers face production disruptions from a potential shortage of Nexperia automotive chips, sparked by the Dutch government taking control of the supplier (owned by China's Wingtech) and China blocking exports of its finished products. Honda Motor became the first known automaker to reduce production as of October 30, 2025. Volkswagen reported supplies are sufficient until at least next week, while Stellantis operates a cross-functional "war room" for daily management. A meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Busan on October 30 yielded no resolution. The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association warned assembly lines could stop within days. The affected legacy semiconductors are used in basic vehicle functions and lack sufficient alternative sources.

Germany's Volkswagen announced on November 5, 2025, it will develop an in-house assisted driving chip for its China business, via a joint venture between software unit CARIAD and Horizon Robotics. This is Volkswagen's first proprietary chip of this kind, part of its "In China, for China" strategy to recapture sagging sales amid rising local brands and trade tensions over semiconductors. Smart driving is a key battleground in China's auto market. CEO Ralf Brandstatter cited mastering core technologies for future mobility. Delivery is expected in three to five years. A spokesman noted the current focus is localized implementation, with potential future alignment to feed achievements back into global operations.

On November 6, 2025, BMW reported rising profitability: its auto unit operating profit margin hit 5.2% in Q3 2025, up from 2.3% a year earlier, with shares surging 6.8% in Frankfurt. Despite slowing Chinese sales, tariffs (EU levies on Chinese-made EVs, US tariffs), and a cut to its 2025 outlook in October, CEO Oliver Zipse cited resilience, aided by a large US footprint—U.S. deliveries rose 25% year-on-year. Net profit was €1.7 billion, sharply up from €476 million in Q3 2024 (impacted by a recall), while revenues remained flat at €32 billion. R&D spending fell significantly. A positive development: China eased its export ban on Nexperia semiconductors, though chip supply remains volatile.

Honda reported a 37% profit decline for April–September 2025, with net profit falling to ¥311.8 billion ($2B) from ¥494.6 billion a year earlier, as US President Donald Trump’s tariffs weighed on the carmaker. Sales dropped 1.5% to ¥10.6 trillion ($69B). Honda lowered its full-year profit forecast to ¥300 billion ($2B), a 64% decline. Tariffs reduced operating profit by ¥164 billion ($1.1B). Unfavorable currency exchange erased ¥116 billion ($756M). Record motorcycle sales (10.7M units) were offset by lower vehicle sales (1.68M vs 1.78M). A chip shortage from the Dutch government’s takeover of Nexperia and China’s temporary chip blockade halted production at Honda’s Celaya, Mexico plant from October 28 and adjusted North American plants from October 27. No restoration date given.

Volkswagen's China chief confirmed that carmakers have received initial chip deliveries from Nexperia after a supply outage. The Dutch government seized control of Nexperia on September 30 amid the U.S.-China trade war, and China blocked its exports from October 4. Under a U.S.-China agreement, Nexperia will not face U.S. export restrictions for one year, and China now grants short-term special permits for case-by-case exports. However, the sustainability of this system depends on U.S.-China relations. While Volkswagen’s China production is currently unaffected, the situation creates uncertainty.

Honda slashed its annual operating profit outlook by a fifth, citing one-off EV costs, a chip shortage from Nexperia, and a ¥385 billion hit from US tariffs. Shares fell 4.7%. The deeper threat is intensifying competition from Chinese EV makers like BYD in Southeast Asia, where Honda has lost pricing and market share. It now expects to sell 925,000 vehicles in Asia (including China), down from a prior 1.09 million, with 75,000 fewer cars sold in Asia outside China versus last year. Retail sales plunged nearly 30% in Indonesia, 18% in Malaysia, and 12% in Thailand. No new models are planned for the region. Honda faces structural challenges: its automotive division posted a third consecutive quarterly operating loss, while motorcycle profits are record high. North American headwinds include a chip-related factory shutdown in Mexico. Merger talks with Nissan had collapsed.

On November 12, 2025, Ford CEO Jim Farley advised aspiring executives to pursue chief supply chain officer (CSCO) roles over CEO, emphasizing that supply chain leaders must grasp technology and geopolitics. He noted that CEOs like Tim Cook and Mary Barra came from supply chain backgrounds. The comments come as automakers face supply chain disruptions from Trump administration tariffs, costing Ford $1 billion and GM $3.5–4.5 billion, and China's rare earth restrictions. Farley also warned of dangerous US dependency on foreign materials and manufacturing job shortages.

Ford F-150 Lightning production remains paused after an aluminum supplier fire, costing Ford $1.5–2 billion in 2025. Employees at Ford World Headquarters inadvertently revealed a second-generation Lightning on LinkedIn, expected to join the next F-150 lineup in late 2027 or 2028. CEO Jim Farley noted demand was lower than expected, with only 23,034 Lightning units sold through October. The supplier outage is projected until Q1 2026, so Lightning production may not restart until mid-2026, potentially remaining halted until the new model arrives. Competitor Ram canceled its electric truck in favor of a range-extender model.

On 2025-11-24, German automakers Volkswagen, BMW, and Mercedes-Benz accelerated efforts to reduce China dependence after the Nexperia crisis—a Dutch chipmaker owned by China's Wingtech—triggered Beijing's export restrictions. The disruption impacted Honda and Bosch, leading the automakers to form internal task forces and instruct suppliers to find permanent alternatives for Chinese semiconductors and raw materials. Analysts estimate replacing China's chips and rare earths will take 3–7 years, and lithium capacity decades. Despite surging investment (EUR4.2 billion in 2023–2024), German brands' China market share dropped from ~25% (2021) to ~10% (2025). They now deepen Chinese R&D partnerships while facing EU pressure to reduce dependence amid costly EV transitions.

In November 2025, Ford and Hyundai reported marginal US sales declines as electric vehicle demand fell after the end of $7,500 federal tax credits under President Trump’s tax bill. Ford’s overall sales slipped nearly 1% to 164,925 units; EV sales (Mustang Mach-E, F-150 Lightning) dropped 61% to 4,247, exacerbated by a fire at a key aluminum supplier’s plant. Hyundai’s overall sales fell 2%; Ioniq 5 and Ioniq 6 sales each declined over 55%. Hyundai CEO noted shoppers shifted to hybrids, which surged 42%. Kia posted a 2.7% gain, while Honda sales fell 15%, hurt by semiconductor shortages. Automakers continue to push EVs despite headwinds.

Volkswagen Group CEO Oliver Blume announced a 160-billion-euro ($186 billion) investment plan through 2030, a reduction from previous periods (165 billion for 2025-2029 and 180 billion for 2024-2028). The spending reflects belt-tightening as Europe's top automaker faces crises in China and the US due to tariffs and fierce competition, hurting profits particularly at Porsche. Blume confirmed the focus is on Germany and Europe across products, technology, and infrastructure. Talks on an extended Porsche savings program will run into 2026. A potential Audi US plant hinges on substantial Washington financial support, while localising production and a tailor-made Porsche model for China remain possible.

Jamie Dimon’s JPMorgan Chase announced on December 8, 2025, an external advisory council for its $1.5 trillion Security and Resilience Initiative (SRI), announced in October. The council includes Jeff Bezos, Michael Dell, Ford CEO Jim Farley, and former officials like Condoleezza Rice and Robert Gates. Farley has warned about U.S. dependence on China for chips and rare earths, citing strategic vulnerability. The SRI will first invest up to $10 billion in equity and venture capital for companies critical to U.S. national security. Todd Combs, a Berkshire Hathaway investment manager, will lead the SRI investment group starting January 2026.

On December 11, 2025, Ford confirmed that its Chinese rare-earth magnet suppliers received the first batch of new streamlined export licenses from Beijing, agreed after Presidents Xi Jinping and Trump met in South Korea. The year-long general permits allow larger shipments with fewer hurdles, replacing the per-shipment licenses imposed in April that caused shortages and halted parts of the auto supply chain. Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul noted German automakers were excluded, raising concerns about preferential U.S. access. BMW is monitoring the licenses, while Volkswagen said its supply is stable and not experiencing shortages. China's rare-earth exports jumped in November. Ford urged continued U.S.-China collaboration to resolve supply chain issues.

Honda Motor will pause vehicle production at several plants in Japan and China due to the global semiconductor shortage. Output in Japan will stop on 5–6 January; which plants are affected is unspecified. In China, all three Guangqi Honda Automobile factories (a joint venture with Guangzhou Automobile Group) will shut from 29 December to 2 January. The fresh suspensions indicate parts availability remains unstable despite recent moves to ease supply constraints. China earlier blocked exports from chipmaker Nexperia, then dropped those curbs in November. Honda, among the manufacturers most affected, has revised its sales outlook down to 3.34 million units from 3.62 million and previously scaled back North American operations. Nexperia produces semiconductors for automotive control systems.

Honda is diversifying semiconductor procurement from suppliers in and outside Japan to reduce dependency on China and buffer against future shortages. The move follows a chip shortage late last year that caused expected losses of hundreds of millions of dollars in operating profit.

Housing starts in Ontario fell to 62,561 in 2025, the lowest since Ford took office in 2018, far below the 150,000 target. Ford also called for eliminating development charges and federal HST to revive the construction and auto sectors.

On March 6, 2026, Aston Martin faced severe issues with its Honda-supplied power units at the F1 Australian Grand Prix. Team principal Adrian Newey announced that two of the team’s four batteries had failed, leaving only two operational units in the cars of Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll. Newey also warned that persistent vibration from the power unit could cause permanent nerve damage to drivers, limiting practice running. Mechanics worked until 4 a.m. to address the problems. On March 13, 2026, Honda announced a $15.7 billion writedown of its EV business, primarily in the U.S., and a write-down of some Chinese operations, leading to its first annual loss in nearly 70 years. The automaker canceled three planned U.S. EV models after President Trump ended EV subsidies, causing demand to crater. Battery EVs comprised only 2.5% of Honda's global sales (84,000 vehicles). Honda will pivot to hybrids in the U.S. and seek growth in India. In China, it faces a widening technological gap with newer EV makers, selling only 17,000 EVs there last year. Analysts raised concerns about long-term competitiveness. The direction of its Sony joint venture remains under discussion.

On March 16, 2026, Honda canceled three new EV model launches and announced a $15.7 billion loss. $8.1 billion will be booked in the current fiscal year ending this month, resulting in Honda's first annual loss in 69 years at $4.3 billion. An additional $7.5 billion loss will be taken in FY ending March 2027. CEO Toshihiro Mibe acknowledged failure to flexibly adapt strategy to shifting market conditions and policy trends, citing changes in hybrid categories, US tariffs, Chinese competition, and new EV entrants as causes.

Volkswagen is shifting away from Nvidia for driver-assist chips in China, instead relying on local partners Horizon Robotics and Xpeng. Production of the ID. UNYX 08, its first all-electric SUV with L2 driver-assist using Xpeng's Turing chip, began March 13, 2026, in Hefei, with deliveries in China by end of June. Volkswagen CTO Thomas Ulbrich stated there is no reason to stick with Nvidia. The company expects L3 capabilities in about two years. Its Carizon joint venture aims to deliver its own chip in three to five years. Despite a 53% profit drop and 8% sales decline, Volkswagen plans 20 new battery or hybrid models in China in 2026, and 50 by 2030 (30 fully electric).

Ford's stock has fallen over 20% from 2026 highs, pushing its dividend yield above 5%. The automaker pays a static quarterly dividend of $0.15 and targets returning 40–50% of free cash flow (FCF) to shareholders, often supplemented by special dividends. In 2025, FCF plunged to $3.5 billion from $6.7 billion in 2024, partly due to tariffs and supply-chain disruptions from a supplier fire. Ford guides 2026 FCF between $5–$6 billion, enough to cover regular dividends. Analysts have a "Hold" consensus; Bank of America recently rated "Buy" with a $17 target, and Piper Sandler upgraded to "Overweight" ($16). The mean target is $13.72. Ford faced a record 153 recalls in 2025 (12.9 million vehicles), with 2026 expected to be equally problematic.

SHM determined it lacked a viable path forward. The discontinuation follows years of AFEELA promotions, including art installations as recent as March 18, and best-of appearances at CES 2023, 2024, and 2026. Rising tech costs from memory and chip shortages driven by AI investments contributed to the shift. The decision eliminates a potential competitor to Tesla and BYD in the EV market.

On October 13, 2025, Chinese semiconductor firm Wingtech announced it will seek help from Chinese government departments after Dutch authorities intervened over its European subsidiary Nexperia. In late September, the Netherlands invoked the Goods Availability Act to take control of Nexperia, citing national security concerns due to "serious governance shortcomings." The Dutch government can now block or reverse Nexperia's decisions while regular production continues. Wingtech is pursuing legal remedies and vowed to protect shareholder interests. Nexperia, acquired by Wingtech in 2018, manufactures chips for everyday goods like cars and refrigerators. The move reflects ongoing semiconductor tensions; Wingtech was placed on a U.S. entity list in December 2024.

On October 14, 2025, the China Semiconductor Industry Association denounced the Dutch government's intervention in Nexperia, a semiconductor firm and overseas subsidiary of Chinese company Wingtech. The association opposed the abuse of "national security" and discriminatory restrictions, warning of harm to the global semiconductor ecosystem. Wingtech condemned the Dutch order under the "Availability of Goods Act" as an overreach driven by geopolitical bias, violating EU market rules. Wingtech noted Nexperia achieved 2.36 billion euros in revenue (2022) and zero-debt operation by October 2024. China's foreign ministry urged against politicizing economic issues. The event signals heightened regulatory risk and potential disruption to semiconductor supply chains.

On October 24, 2025, Nexperia’s Chinese parent Wingtech Technology warned the Dutch government that failure to restore control of seized chipmaking unit Nexperia before end-2025 could temporarily pressure revenue, profit, and cash flow. The Dutch government seized Nexperia last month amid mounting US pressure after Wingtech was added to the US Entity List in 2024, citing independence concerns and removing Nexperia’s Chinese CEO. Despite a 12.2% year-on-year rise in semiconductor revenue in Q3 2025, Wingtech doubts long-term growth. China’s commerce minister said the seizure “seriously affected” global supply chain stability; the Dutch government aims for a constructive solution.

On October 30, 2025, Toyota CEO Koji Sato stated at the Japan Mobility Show that the automaker faces no immediate chip shortage from China’s export curbs on Dutch semiconductor firm Nexperia, but acknowledged potential production risks if restrictions persist. Sato added that Toyota is monitoring supply chains closely. The curbs followed the Dutch government’s seizure of Nexperia, citing national security risks tied to its Chinese parent, Wingtech, prompting Beijing’s export restrictions. Sato noted Japanese manufacturers are working to standardize legacy chips to avoid a repeat of pandemic-era shortages.

China’s Ministry of Commerce urged the Netherlands to “stop interfering” in Nexperia’s internal affairs and to find a constructive solution, according to a statement on Bloomberg Terminal. The dispute centers on Nexperia, a supplier of doped electronic materials (HS4 3818), and has escalated into a broader supply-chain issue affecting automotive production.

China responded on October 4 by halting exports of Nexperia's finished products, a measure it later relaxed. Dutch Economy Minister Vincent Karremans called the suspension a gesture of goodwill and said talks will continue. He expressed positivity about Chinese measures to ensure chip supply to Europe. Nexperia is a major supplier of basic chips to the car industry; the dispute caused shortages threatening automotive supply chains and leading to production slowdowns.

However, the decision left unresolved fundamental questions over export controls, technology transfer, and national security, signaling that underlying geopolitical tensions persist.
